newsitem.title: SPAIN: U.S. leaders to take NATO message across Europe.
newsitem.headline: U.S. leaders to take NATO message across Europe.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and other American leaders fan out across former communist Europe on Thursday to accept accolades from states invited to join NATO and assure those left out they have not been abandoned.

Clinton, accompanied by Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, flies first to the Polish capital Warsaw where he will be feted by crowds delighted their country has joined one of the West's leading clubs, bidding a final farewell to its Soviet-imposed communist past.

Poland, which won a place alongside Hungary and the Czech Republic in the first round of the alliance's eastwards push, was invaded by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union in 1939, the latest attack in a history of domination by powerful neighbours.
Ecstatic Polish commentators have called the invitation to join the Western military alliance one of the most important moments in the last 300 years of its history.

A five-hour event on the Warsaw Old Town's Castle Square on Thursday, featuring country, jazz and folk music of the two nations, will culminate in a 15-minute address by Clinton. Organisers expect some 20,000 people to attend.

Since emerging from Soviet domination in 1991, the country has yearned to come under the mutual defence commitment of NATO's 1949 founding treaty which places the European allies under the cover of the American nuclear shield.
Justifying the decision to extend U.S. protection to the new democracies, Clinton said they now shared the values and aspirations of the free world.
"It is a pretty good gamble, after all no NATO state has ever been attacked," Clinton told a news conference after a two-day NATO summit in Madrid launched the historic enlargement.
Clinton, who must have the decision ratified by the Republican-led U.S. Congress, refused to buckle to European pressure to let Romania and Slovenia join in the first wave.

But after a day of intense wrangling with French President Jacques Chirac and others on Tuesday, he agreed the two states should get favourable mention in the final communique as serious candidates next time the situation is reviewed in 1999.
On Wednesday, the French leader told a news conference he was sure NATO would invite the two countries to join when it marks its 50th anniversary with a summit in two years time.

The three future NATO members and the also-rans now look to the European Union for their next step towards integration into the prosperous West. The European Commission is due to recommend next week how many qualify for entry negotiations, but the 20 commissioners are divided on not dissimilar lines to NATO.
From Warsaw, Clinton will fly on to Bucharest to explain the NATO decision to Romanians and urge them to continue the reform process that brought them so close on this occasion.

Albright will take the same message to Slovenia and the former Soviet republic of Lithuania which failed to win mention by name in the communique but was happy with a broader reference to the importance NATO gives to the Baltic region.
Albright will also visit St Petersburg to encourage Russia to take full advantage of the possibilities of a special pact with NATO, negotiated to run in parallel with enlargement.
Moscow has accepted it is powerless to stop enlargement, but the sight of its former Warsaw Pact satellites joining the organisation which won the Cold War is a bitter pill to swallow.

Deputy Prime Minister Valery Serov, who represented Russia in Madrid, reasserted its strong opposition to the alliance's eastward thrust, on Wednesday telling reporters: "The expansion of NATO presents more problems than answers."
Serov was attending the inaugural meeting on the summit's second day of a new security council of 28 non-NATO nations spanning North America, Europe and former Soviet Asia.
Alliance leaders see the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council, along with cooperation charters with Russia and Ukraine, as essential elements in a emerging new European security order.
Albright, whose family fled Czechoslovakia twice, to escape the Nazis and the communists, then moves on to her birth place Prague for what is certain to be an emotional visit.
After the summit decision, she said she was pleased at the invitations to Poland and Hungary, but the one to Czech Republic particularly warmed her heart.
"It makes me feel that I've been part of history," she said.
Meanwhile, U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen will visit Hungary, the third successful candidate, Bulgaria and Ukraine.

NATO also on Wednesday signed a sweeping new security charter with Ukraine, sealing the Slav nation's shift away from the former Soviet sphere of influence and closer to the Western orbit -- an attempt to answer their security concerns without alarming Russia.
